package_info.why_malicious: The package is part of a large-scale, coordinated spam campaign designed to exploit the Tea protocol's reward system. Thousands of nearly identical, non-functional or minimally functional packages are published under random names, each with artificially inflated dependency graphs, solely to increase 'teaRank' and farm cryptocurrency rewards. This behavior pollutes the open source ecosystem, increases the risk of supply chain attacks, and undermines trust in package repositories by flooding them with low-quality, interconnected packages.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At publish-time, the package.json file declares thousands of dependencies on other spam packages from the same campaign, creating a dense, artificially interconnected dependency graph to manipulate the Tea protocol's ranking algorithm and inflate teaRank scores.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Legitimate npm packages almost never declare thousands of dependencies, especially on obscure or non-functional packages. This pattern is highly indicative of automated, coordinated spam designed to game ranking systems.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages declare only necessary dependencies required for their functionality. Here, dependencies are used solely to manipulate ranking algorithms, not for any technical necessity or utility.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some large meta-packages or frameworks may have many dependencies, but not in this random, interconnected, and non-functional manner, nor with such a high volume of obscure packages.
key_indicators: package.json with thousands of dependencies, often on other low-quality or recently published packages
Dependencies form a dense, interconnected network among spam packages
No meaningful code or utility present in the package

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At publish-time, the tea.yaml file is included in the package to register it with the Tea protocol, associating it with a unique codeOwner address and enabling the package to participate in the reward system and receive TEA tokens.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The presence of tea.yaml in thousands of low-quality, randomly named packages is a clear indicator of automated registration for reward farming, rather than legitimate project registration.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate projects use tea.yaml to register real, valuable open source projects for Tea protocol rewards. In this case, it is used to mass-register spam packages with no real utility.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate open source projects may use tea.yaml to participate in the Tea protocol for compensation, but not at this scale or with such low-quality, non-functional packages.
key_indicators: tea.yaml present in every spam package, regardless of actual project value
Unique codeOwner addresses for each spam package, often with no real project or community
Automated, mass inclusion of tea.yaml across thousands of packages

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At publish-time, a minimal or meaningless README.md file is included, containing only the package name or random text, to fulfill repository requirements without providing any documentation or utility.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: README.md files are expected to provide documentation and usage instructions. Here, they are empty or contain only the package name or random, meaningless text, indicating automated, non-genuine publication.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages provide meaningful documentation in README.md. Spam packages include only placeholder or nonsensical content, failing to inform users or developers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Initial scaffolding of new projects may have minimal README files, but not at this scale or with such consistently meaningless content.
key_indicators: README.md with only the package name or random, contextless text
No actual documentation, usage instructions, or project information
Pattern of minimal README.md files across thousands of packages

behavioral_signatures: Packages with thousands of dependencies, especially on other obscure, low-download, or recently published packages
Presence of tea.yaml in non-functional or minimal packages
Mass publication of packages with random, hyphenated names or Latin portmanteaus
Minimal or meaningless README.md files with only the package name or random text
file_indicators: tea.yaml present in the root directory of the package
package.json with more than 100 dependencies, especially if dependencies are also low-quality or recently published
README.md containing only the package name or random, contextless text
network_indicators: High volume of npm publish events from the same IP address or API key within a short time frame
Automated creation of GitHub repositories with minimal or no content, often linked to the published npm packages
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages with unusually high numbers of dependencies, particularly when dependencies are also low-quality, obscure, or recently published. Flag packages containing tea.yaml when combined with minimal code and documentation. Detect mass publication patterns, such as many packages from the same user, IP, or with similar naming schemes. Correlate with automated GitHub account creation and repository population. Use heuristics to identify interconnected spam networks and artificially inflated dependency graphs. Cross-reference codeOwner addresses in tea.yaml files to detect mass registration for reward farming.
